sections.h2: Selling fast in Troy without months of showings
sections.html:
Troy sellers who want speed have two main choices: an as-is cash purchase, or a listing priced to move. The right one follows the house. A downtown address inside the Historic District raises different questions than a recent subdivision home, so figure out where yours stands first.

  • Agent listing: reaches Dayton-area buyers, with an inspection and loan approval still ahead of closing.
  • Owner-handled sale: you draft the contract, deliver the disclosure form and arrange the deed.
  • Direct as-is purchase: the buyer takes on the repairs, and you set closing to fit your move.

The finish is the same on every route. The deed clears the Miami County Engineer and Auditor, then goes to the Recorder.

Troy is the Miami County seat and its largest city, on the Great Miami River about 19 miles north of Dayton. It's growing: the estimate is 27,344 residents, up 3.8 percent from the April 2020 base, and every census from 1990 to 2020 counted more people than the last.

The 2020 census counted 11,859 housing units, 5.6 percent of them empty.

The older core is distinctive. Overfield Tavern, from 1808, is now a museum, and the Troy-Hayner Cultural Center fills a 1914 Romanesque mansion. The Hobart Welded Steel House Company built just 22 prefabricated steel houses, every one in Troy, and 16 survive on the National Register of Historic Places.

The Historic District is an overlay running roughly from the Miami River on the north to Canal Street on the south, and from Oxford Street on the west to Clay Street on the east. The Planning Commission reviews alterations there, so check before you repaint, reside or replace windows for a sale.

sections.h2: Which school district is the house in?
sections.html: Most of Troy belongs to Troy City Schools. A slice of the city falls in the Miami East Local School District, so verify the district for your exact address before you advertise it. Buyers with children will ask.

The city enforces the International Property Maintenance Code on existing homes and other structures, and ignoring it can bring penalties from the courts. Property maintenance staff log complaints and also spot problems on their own. Troy publishes an exterior checklist. Walk your property with it before you list to catch peeling paint, broken steps or overgrown yards.

If you added a shed, deck, garage or pool, ask the city's Planning and Zoning Division whether the zoning permit was finished. A buyer's inspector or lender may ask for the paper trail.

sections.h2: Water service lines and utility transfer
sections.html:
Troy houses built before February 1, 1944 could have lead water service lines, since the city banned lead in 1944. Under the EPA's Lead and Copper Rule, the city is inventorying service line materials and mails owners of those homes a yearly letter until the line is replaced or its material is verified. A city technician can inspect in about 15 minutes on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. (937-335-4151), or you can self-report online.

For the buyer, the Utility Billing office at City Hall, 100 S. Market Street, opens service with photo ID plus a deed, closing papers or an accepted purchase contract. Any delinquency must be cleared first. Settle your own account and call the office about the handover.

Standards Miami County adopted on August 12, 2025 set the sequence. The Engineer's office approves the instrument first. The Auditor then takes a completed DTE 100 statement of value or a DTE 100 EX exemption form. The Recorder files a deed only after it carries both approval stamps.

  • Seller names on the deed must match the previous deed, or an affidavit under Ohio Revised Code 5301.252 has to explain the gap in title.
  • A land contract needs Engineer approval and an Auditor date stamp before it is recorded.
  • Fee checks go to the Miami County Auditor for the exact amount, because overpayments are refused.
  • The Auditor's website has a conveyance fee calculator that adds in the parcel transfer fee.

Ohio Revised Code 322.02 puts the county transfer tax on the grantor. The same standards cover next-of-kin affidavits, survivorship transfers and transfer on death affidavits, which helps when a Troy house comes from an estate.

sections.h2: When a direct sale suits a Troy house
sections.html:
Three kinds of Troy property tend to fit. One is a pre-1944 house with an unverified water line and old systems. Another is a rental, since about 34.5 percent of occupied Troy homes aren't owner-occupied. The third is an estate house where the heirs live elsewhere.

In each case, ask the buyer in writing who handles the lead line inventory, any open permit and the county transfer paperwork. Keep a copy of the signed purchase contract for the utility office.

Under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, a buyer who first sees the property disclosure form after signing may rescind in writing within three business days of receipt. That right ends 30 days after acceptance or at closing, whichever is earlier. A buyer who received the form before making an offer has no rescission right.

Hand over the form with the first showing packet. A seller who inherited the house and did not live in it during the prior year is exempt.

Start with the house itself. Find out whether it sits in the Historic District, whether it predates 1944, and whether any shed, deck or pool lacks a finished permit. Those three answers drive most of what comes later, and each one is a single call to the city.

Next, gather the paperwork. Pull the previous deed so the seller names match, and decide whether an affidavit is needed. Ask your attorney or title company for the DTE 100 or DTE 100 EX and run your price through the Auditor's calculator so there are no surprises on closing day.

Last, plan the handover. The buyer will need photo ID and the closing papers at the Utility Billing office, and you'll want your own account settled. Whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan, these steps stay the same. A cash buyer simply removes the loan approval and appraisal wait from the schedule.

faqs.q: Where do I file a deed for a Troy house?
faqs.a: Miami County handles it. The Engineer approves the description, the Auditor processes the conveyance form, and the Recorder files the deed. Begin with the Engineer.

faqs.q: Does Troy have a historic district that limits changes?
faqs.a: Inside the overlay, yes: the Planning Commission reviews alterations. The district is generally bounded by the Miami River, Clay, Canal and Oxford streets, and Planning and Zoning can tell you if your address is in it.

faqs.q: Will an old Troy home need a lead service line inspection?
faqs.a: Only homes built before February 1, 1944 are in the inventory. Those owners receive a yearly letter until the line is replaced or its material is confirmed by inspection or self-report.

faqs.q: Who pays the conveyance fee when a Troy house sells?
faqs.a: You do, as grantor, under Ohio Revised Code 322.02. Run your sale price through the Miami County Auditor's online calculator, which includes the parcel transfer fee, before the closing date.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Troy house with unpermitted work?
faqs.a: Yes, though a buyer's inspector may ask about permits. Check with Planning and Zoning on any shed, deck or pool, and document or correct it before you list.
